key_concept: Electron gain enthalpy grows more negative as atomic size decreases down to Cl, but F is anomalous: its very small 2p shell causes strong electron–electron repulsion, so Cl releases the most energy among the halogens.
steps: The question compares the magnitude of negative electron gain enthalpy, i.e. how much energy is released when $X(g) + e^- \rightarrow X^-(g)$.
Down the group from Cl to I, atomic size increases. The incoming electron is held less firmly by the nucleus, so less energy is released: $Cl > Br > I$.
F is the exception. Its compact $2p$ subshell is already crowded, so the added electron feels strong interelectronic repulsion. This makes $|\Delta_{eg}H|$ of F smaller than that of Cl.
Br ($-325$) is only slightly less negative than F ($-328$), so F still sits above Br.
Combining these gives the order $Cl > F > Br > I$ (by magnitude of energy released).
why_not_others: Option (1) applies the simple size trend and ignores fluorine's electron–electron repulsion anomaly. Options (2) and (4) wrongly place the larger Br or I above Cl.
common_trap: Assuming fluorine, being the most electronegative element, must also have the most negative electron gain enthalpy.
time_saving_tip: Remember the rule 'Cl has the highest electron gain enthalpy in the periodic table'. Only option (3) starts with Cl.
